conventions.convention: The kernel is k(z,w)=log(1/|z−w|), with diagonal value +∞. For finite positive compactly supported Borel measures, Uμ integrates k and pμ=−Uμ integrates log|z−w|. U0=p0=I(0)=0; mixed energy is zero if either measure is zero.
For nonempty compact K, VK is the infimum of energy over Borel probability measures carried by K, and cap(K)=exp(−VK), with exp(−∞)=0. The empty set has capacity zero.

Capacity-polarity tests every compact subset of a set. Quasi-everywhere assertions use a Borel capacity-polar exceptional set. The subharmonic-polar notion is separately defined; the Evans lemma proves equivalence for compact sets and specified countable unions of compact sets.
The Riesz normalization is μu=(2π)−1Δu, with Δ=∂x²+∂y². Thus Δpμ=2πμ and ΔUμ=−2πμ. The cited distribution convention uses complex-linear test-function pairings without conjugation.

Chebyshev extremal norms concern monic polynomials of degree n≥1. Fekete diameters start at n=2. Empty-set constants are specified separately, and finite sets eventually have zero extremal norms and zero Fekete diameters.
Proper discontinuity means that for every compact K only finitely many group elements satisfy gK∩K≠∅. Freeness is a separate requirement.
Surface harmonicity and subharmonicity are chartwise. The underlying Riemann surfaces are nonempty, connected, Hausdorff and second countable; harmonic functions are real-valued.

The canonical surface envelope is the supremum of nonnegative subharmonic, compactly supported functions with at most a unit logarithmic pole. Its finite kernel has sign −log|z| at the pole. On compact surfaces the support K=X is expressly allowed.
The surface Poincaré metric is pulled back locally from the universal covering disc with length element 2|dz|/(1−|z|²), giving curvature −1 and distance 2 artanh|φz(w)|.
A hypersurface equation is a nonzero nonunit holomorphic germ. It is reduced exactly when no irreducible square divides it. Germs at p are transported to the origin by z↦p+z.
The branch set belongs to a fixed prepared projection and is the zero set of its discriminant in the base. It need not equal the image of the hypersurface singular locus.

Regularity uses a local reduced equation: a hypersurface point is regular exactly when its differential is nonzero. Smoothness of an individual component does not establish regularity of their union at an intersection.

Puiseux coordinates may change by an invertible complex-linear map. Primitivity means minimal first-coordinate exponent in the same coordinates; the constructed form is (t^m,h(t)) with h containing only powers greater than m.

Normalisation takes integral closure inside the localisation at all nonzerodivisors. In the normalisation corollary, C((t)) explicitly denotes Frac(C{t}), the convergent meromorphic germ field, rather than the formal Laurent-series field.

load_bearing.statement: For n≥1, a reduced nonzero nonunit germ regular in the last variable of order d has preparation f=uW whose polynomial W is square-free over Frac(O(n−1,0)), with that field interpreted as C when n=1. Consequently Disc(W) is a nonzero holomorphic base germ.

For n≥1 and a reduced nonzero nonunit germ at p, an invertible linear change of centred coordinates gives a Weierstrass polynomial W of degree d≥1 and a product representative V×D with the same zero set. Its projection to V is proper, surjective and finite; O(n,0)/(W) is a finite O(n−1,0)-module; off Disc(W)=0 the projection is a d-sheeted holomorphic covering. For n=1 the base is a point.
For complex domains Ω1,Ω2, a biholomorphism G:Ω1→Ω2 and u:Ω2→[−∞,∞), u is subharmonic on Ω2 if and only if u∘G is subharmonic on Ω1.

For n≥1, p∈C^n and a nonzero nonunit germ f, write f=u∏q_i^{e_i} with pairwise nonassociate irreducibles and e_i≥1. The product f_red=∏q_i is reduced, its associate class depends only on f, and representatives of f and f_red have the same zero set near p.
For n≥1, p∈C^n and a reduced nonzero nonunit germ f, I_p(Z(f))=(f). More generally, for any nonzero nonunit germ g, I_p(Z(g))=(g_red).

Assume Countable Choice. For a Riemann surface X and p∈X, its canonical Perron envelope is either +∞ everywhere off p or finite everywhere off p. In the finite case it is strictly positive and harmonic off p, g+log|z| extends harmonically across p in every centred chart, and g is bounded above by every positive harmonic function off p with a unit logarithmic pole at p.

Assume Countable Choice. If X admits finite canonical Green kernels at distinct p,q, then g_X(p,q)=g_X(q,p). On a noncompact X, a regular exhaustion containing p,q in its first domain has finite zero-boundary kernels with unit logarithmic poles; those kernels increase and converge pointwise to g_X(·,p) whenever that canonical kernel is finite.

Assume Countable Choice. For finite positive compactly supported Borel measures μ,ν of equal mass and finite logarithmic energies, their mixed energy is finite, I(μ−ν)=I(μ)−2I(μ,ν)+I(ν) is a real number, and I(μ−ν)≥0 with equality if and only if μ−ν=0. The zero-mass case is included.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For nonempty compact K⊂C with cap(K)>0, exactly one Borel probability measure μK on K satisfies I(μK)=VK=inf_{μ∈P(K)}I(μ)<+∞. If cap(K)=0, every μ∈P(K) has infinite energy and no equilibrium measure is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. For a finite positive compactly supported Borel measure μ with support S, pμ is locally integrable and subharmonic on C, harmonic on C∖S, and Δpμ=2πμ, equivalently ΔUμ=−2πμ, distributionally. The zero measure is included.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For compact K⊂C with cap(K)>0 and its equilibrium measure μK, UμK(z)≤VK for every z∈C, and UμK=VK outside a Borel capacity-polar subset of K. The exceptional set may be a countable union of compact capacity-zero sets.

Assume Dependent Choice. A compact E⊂C has capacity zero if and only if it lies in the −∞ locus of a subharmonic function on a domain containing E. The forward witness can be global; for nonempty E it can be −Uσ for a finite positive measure carried by E. The same witness construction and converse apply to a specified sequence of compact capacity-zero sets and their union, without asserting an arbitrary-set equivalence.

Assume Countable Choice. A locally uniformly bounded sequence of real harmonic functions on a Riemann surface has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset to a harmonic function. For plane harmonic functions converging as distributions, the limiting distribution is harmonic and has a harmonic representative.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every simply connected Riemann surface is biholomorphic to exactly one of the Riemann sphere, the complex plane and the unit disc.

An irreducible plane hypersurface germ at 0, with reduced equation, admits an invertible complex-linear coordinate change and an injective holomorphic parametrisation γ(t)=(t^m,h(t)), m≥1, with h(t)=∑_{k>m}a_k t^k and image germ exactly X. Primitivity means minimal first-coordinate exponent in these same coordinates. Primitive parametrisations are injective, and two with first component t^m differ by t↦ζt, ζ^m=1.

concerns.concern: The Sharpness remark says the inequality inf_K Uσ≤VK 'becomes an equality for σ=μK, since UμK=VK quasi-everywhere on K'. Quasi-everywhere equality does not imply this ordinary infimum equality. Take K=the closed unit disc ∪{2}. Every finite-energy probability gives the isolated point zero mass, so μK is the circular equilibrium measure and VK=0, while UμK(2)=−log 2. Thus inf_K UμK=−log 2<0. The proposition's inequality is unaffected, but the asserted sharpness on every such K is false.

The Definition states 'The value is a real number' for every φ∈Cc∞(Ω), while its cited def-distribution fixes a complex-linear test space. For u(z)=|z|² and φ=iψ with real compactly supported ψ having positive integral, μu(φ)=(2i/π)∫ψ is nonreal. Real-valuedness requires real-valued tests.

Facts F2 repeats that μu(φ) is 'a real number by local integrability of u' for every φ∈Cc∞(Ω). Local integrability ensures finiteness, not real-valuedness on the complex test space. This inherits the domain error in def-riesz-measure-subharmonic-function.

The Scope remark says 'on a disc chart the surface metric restricts to the disc metric itself'. This is false for an arbitrary disc chart. On X=D, take U=D(0,r), 0<r<1, with coordinate ζ=z/r. The surface metric becomes 2r|dζ|/(1−r²|ζ|²), whereas the intrinsic metric of the coordinate unit disc is 2|dζ|/(1−|ζ|²). The universal-cover pullback definition is sound; the chart remark needs a qualification.

Verification 3.2 concludes: 'Every point of each branch is therefore a holomorphic hypersurface graph point, hence a regular point of X by [F5].' Each branch contains the origin, but X is their union and is singular there, as step 4.1 correctly computes. Smoothness of a component is not the cited graph criterion for the union.

Verification 1.1 overstates the holomorphic implicit function theorem: it asserts X0∩(A×C)={(x,η(x)):x∈A} near y0≠0, and X0∩(C×B)={(ψj(y),y):y∈B} at (aj,0). The first set also contains the opposite square-root sheet; the second contains all six points (ak,0). The cited theorem supplies a graph in a small product neighbourhood of the selected point, not in either entire coordinate cylinder. The subsequent atlas construction relies on those incorrectly specified neighbourhoods.

Example clauses 3–4 identify the segment joining two points with the entire part of its orthogonal circle or line inside D or H; that intersection is a complete geodesic, whereas the segment is only the arc between the endpoints. The verification later uses the endpoint-bounded arc correctly. Separately, Verification 2.3 writes φz(ev)=e(z ē−v)/(1−overline(ze)v). The denominator should be 1−z̄ev=1−overline(z ē)v; the displayed intermediate identity fails, for example with z=1/2 and e=i.

Verification 2.3 claims both near and tail logarithmic integrals 'have finite positive and negative parts'. At an atom aj contained in the near measure, the near negative part is infinite, exactly as step 2.2 proves. The decomposition is still legitimate because the near positive part and the tail integral are finite; the asserted finiteness of both parts is false.

Steps 7.1 and 10.1 invoke Countable Choice to fix successive nested subsequences, although each admissible choice set depends on the preceding chosen subsequence. Countable Choice alone does not justify that dependent selection as written; an explicit canonical extraction would preserve the stated hypothesis. Also step 6.1 chooses c_{k,i} merely in V_i^k, while step 7.1 bounds these centres by M_K and step 9.1 applies a bound stated only for pairs in K∩V_i^k. Choosing the already available centres x_i∈K resolves the latter gap.

Verification 7.1 applies the harmonic subsequence theorem successively on countably many discs and invokes Countable Choice for the resulting dependent diagonal selections. As in its weak-harmonic-limit supplier, a canonical extraction rule is needed to justify this under the stated Countable Choice hypothesis rather than an unspoken dependent-choice assumption.

Verification 13.1 says '[F8] permits differentiation under the integral twice'. F8 is the positive C0-functional representation theorem, not a differentiation theorem. The stated logarithmic-moment and derivative bounds support the step, but the cited fact does not. The actual differentiation-under-the-integral supplier is opened and used correctly in the countable-polar-set example.

Verification 2.2 calls Ωε={z∈Ω:B(z,3ε)⊂Ω} an open set. With open balls this need not be open: for the unit disc it is the closed disc |z|≤1−3ε when 0<3ε<1. The convolution is smooth on a larger genuinely open safe region, so the argument is readily recovered by using a strict distance condition or requiring the closed 3ε-ball to lie in Ω.

Facts F4 gives endpoint-preserving reparametrisation homotopies using (1−t)s+tφ(s) with 'φ(0)=0=φ(1)'. At s=1 this equals 1−t, so the endpoint is not preserved. The intended endpoint condition is φ(0)=0 and φ(1)=1.

Verification 2.3 evaluates z⁻¹(ζ) for ζ∈∂D and compares its value with boundary values on ∂U. A centred chart z:U→D is only defined on U, and compactness of its closure does not assert a continuous inverse extension to the unit circle. One can use a smaller coordinate disc whose chart extends past its closure, or supply a cluster-point boundary argument, then transfer the local pole conclusion to every centred chart.

Verification 2.1 derives B=X∖closure(A∪U) and then says 'Thus B is both open and closed'. That displayed equality establishes openness only. Closedness follows from the disjoint boundary traces and the fact that B is relatively closed in Y, but that extra inference is omitted.

Verification 1.2 calls the sphere second countable '(as a metrizable space)'. Metrizability alone does not imply second countability. Here the conclusion follows immediately from S² being a subspace of R³, or from its finite chart cover, so the parenthetical justification should identify that additional fact.

Verification 12.1 begins 'The order of g is 0, or at least m', then explains that its first case means g≡0. The zero function does not have order zero under the usual zero-order convention; the useful assertion is simply 'g≡0 or ord₀g≥m', which the rest of the step proves.
